name: freesasa
why: Solvent accessible surface area calculation is real structural biophysics you can run on protein files at home.

brief.what_it_is: FreeSASA is a command line tool, C library and Python module that calculates solvent accessible surface area (SASA) of biomolecules. The command-line tool takes a PDB file and prints SASA results, using default parameters with no configuration needed. Advanced users can set every calculation parameter, supply their own atomic radii and classifications through configuration files, and call the C or Python APIs on arrays of coordinates. The GitHub README describes the core as a C library with a C++ command line tool, while the homepage lists all three pieces.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames it as a tool that lets casual users get SASA from a PDB file with no configuration overhead, while still giving advanced users full control over parameters and API access. The README says it is designed to be simple to use with defaults but allows customization of all parameters.
brief.how_it_works: By default it uses Lee and Richards' algorithm, with Shrake and Rupley's also available, and both can be parameterized to arbitrary precision. Each atom gets a radius and a polar or apolar class: by default the ProtOr radii from Tsai et al. 1999 for standard amino acids and nucleic acids, and the element's van der Waals radius for other atoms. Users can override these with configuration files, and the share/ directory includes a NACCESS-parameter example.

brief.install_notes: Building from source needs ./configure, make and make install, with autoreconf -i first if you cloned git instead of downloading a tarball. Dependencies for the standard build are json-c and libxml2; the README says these can be turned off with --disable-json and --disable-xml. The Ubuntu prerequisites are git, build-essential, autoconf and libc++ packages, and the full build with unit tests also needs check, libjson-c-dev and libxml2-dev. RHEL and CentOS need the development group plus json-c-devel and libxml2-devel, and CentOS 7 needs a newer GCC from Software Collections. No accounts or hardware are needed. The Python module is a separate repository and package. Prebuilt binaries are available through Homebrew, conda, mamba and pixi.
brief.standout: It is a small, dependency-light C tool that works with a single PDB file out of the box, but it also exposes configurable radii, selectable algorithms and a documented C API. The homepage offers a WebAssembly demo that runs in the browser, so you can try it without installing anything.
brief.status: unknown. Neither the homepage nor the README gives a release date or last-commit date, and the fetch tool did not return repository metadata. The README references version 2.x and a CHANGELOG.md, a Zenodo DOI and a Python module that is packaged separately, and it notes that version 2 broke some of the 1.x API, which suggests active upkeep but does not confirm it.
brief.caveats: The README says the Windows CLI build through MinGW or Cygwin is untested, and MSVC support covers only the C API with no project files. Building from source can be painful on older RHEL/CentOS, and CentOS 7 needs a newer GCC. The Homebrew formula name differs between the homepage (brewsci/bio tap) and the README (plain freesasa). The tool's own description also varies: C library with a C++ CLI in the README, versus CLI, C library and Python module on the homepage. Version 2 changed the API, so older code may break. Licensing is MIT, but the bundled Gemmi third-party code is MPL.

judge.reason: It turns ordinary protein structures into a hands-on structural-biophysics experiment, exposing how geometric algorithms and atomic radii shape solvent-accessible surface calculations.

entry.title: FreeSASA
entry.tldr: Give it a protein structure file and it reports how much of each atom's surface a water molecule could touch, using a rolling-ball algorithm from the 1970s.
entry.deeper_look:
FreeSASA calculates solvent accessible surface area (SASA) for biomolecules. Imagine rolling a ball the size of a water molecule over the surface of a protein. The path the ball's center traces out is the accessible surface. Its area says which parts of a molecule sit exposed to the surrounding water and which are buried in the core.

The command-line tool takes a PDB file, the standard format for 3D structures of proteins and nucleic acids, and prints results with no configuration. By default it uses Lee and Richards' algorithm, with Shrake and Rupley's as an alternative. Each atom gets a radius and a polar or apolar label, taken by default from the ProtOr radii (Tsai et al., 1999). Atoms outside standard amino acids and nucleic acids fall back to the element's van der Waals radius.

The project's own pitch is that casual users get answers with sensible defaults, while advanced users can change every parameter, supply their own radii and classification files, and call a C library or Python module on raw coordinate arrays. The share/ directory includes an example using NACCESS parameters.

The idea underneath is that buried versus exposed surface is a quantity you can compute from coordinates alone, and it connects to real questions in structural biology, such as which residues hydrophobic cores hide and where binding might happen. It is a small way into that field's tooling.
entry.install:
brew install freesasa
# The homepage instead lists: brew install brewsci/bio/freesasa
# No account or hardware needed. You will need a PDB file to feed it. The homepage also offers a WebAssembly demo that runs in the browser.

entry.whats_unique: It works on a single PDB file with zero configuration, yet exposes selectable algorithms, custom radii and a documented C API underneath. The browser demo lets you try it before installing anything.
entry.caveats: Upkeep status is unclear from the sources, and version 2 broke parts of the 1.x API, so older code written against it may not work.
